prompt:
Write a narrative account of about 1,200 words of the Apollo 13 accident and the crew's return to Earth. The reader is a general reader.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.

text:
Apollo 13 left Cape Kennedy on April 11, 1970, carrying James Lovell, Fred Haise and Jack Swigert toward what was meant to be the third landing on the Moon, and for two days it was so uneventful that the television broadcast the crew sent home on the evening of April 13 was not carried by the major American networks. Lovell, the commander, was already a veteran of four spaceflights and was expected to walk on the Fra Mauro highlands with Haise, while Swigert, who had joined the crew only days before launch when Ken Mattingly was grounded after exposure to German measles, remained in lunar orbit aboard the command module Odyssey. The lunar module that would carry the other two to the surface was named Aquarius, and it was still docked to Odyssey, folded against the nose of the spacecraft, when a flight controller in Houston asked the crew to stir the supercold oxygen and hydrogen in the service module's tanks, a routine chore meant to keep the contents from stratifying and giving false quantity readings.

The stir was performed about fifty-six hours into the flight, with the spacecraft roughly two hundred thousand miles from Earth, and a few minutes later a bang rang through the cabin and the spacecraft shuddered. Swigert said that they had had a problem, Lovell repeated it for the controllers, and the voltage on one of the main electrical buses began to fall. The cause was an oxygen tank in the service module that had ruptured. Its history went back years before the flight: the tank had been dropped slightly during handling at the factory, and during a countdown test on the ground its heater thermostats had been exposed to a higher voltage than they were designed to carry, which fused their contacts shut and left the heaters able to run unchecked. Nobody noticed at the time that the Teflon insulation on the wires inside the tank had been scorched, and when Swigert flipped the switch to stir the tank, a spark in that bare wiring ignited the insulation in pure oxygen, the pressure rose until the tank failed, and the blast tore away an entire panel of the service module and crippled the neighbouring tank as well.

In the cabin the crew could see only gauges falling and, through the window, a cloud of venting gas glittering around the ship, and Lovell, looking out, reported that something was escaping into space. Within about three hours both oxygen tanks were empty, and because the fuel cells that made the spacecraft's electricity needed oxygen to run, the command module was dying with them. Houston, under flight director Gene Kranz and later his colleagues on other shifts, quickly concluded that a landing on the Moon was out of the question and that the only objective left was to bring three men home alive. The crew moved into Aquarius, which had its own batteries, its own oxygen and its own engine, and which was designed to support two men for roughly two days on the lunar surface, not three men for four days in deep space. Odyssey was powered down almost completely to preserve its batteries for the single most demanding task still ahead, the re-entry into Earth's atmosphere.

The path home was not obvious, because the spacecraft had been steering on a trajectory that would not have brought it back to Earth had nothing been done, and the large engine in the service module could not be trusted after the explosion. Controllers weighed swinging around the Moon against turning back at once, and chose the loop around the far side, which was safer for the structure of the ship, and about five hours after the explosion Lovell fired the descent engine of the lunar module to put the spacecraft back on a path that would return it to Earth. After passing behind the Moon, at an altitude of a little less than two hundred miles, the three men broke the distance record for human travel, reaching about 248,655 miles from home. A second burn of the same engine shortly after that made the trip faster and shifted the splashdown point to the Pacific, where recovery ships were waiting.

The hours that followed were a lesson in how thin the margin could become. The lunar module's air was kept breathable by canisters of lithium hydroxide that absorbed the carbon dioxide the crew exhaled, but they were nearly exhausted, and the spare canisters in the command module were square while the sockets in Aquarius were round. Engineers in Houston spread out on a table the same odds and ends that were aboard the spacecraft, including plastic bags, cardboard from a flight manual, hoses from the spacesuits and a great deal of duct tape, and read the assembly instructions up to the crew, who built an adapter that let the square canister work in the round fitting, and the carbon dioxide reading fell back into the safe range. Meanwhile the cabin grew bitterly cold as the electrical systems that gave off heat were switched off, with temperatures dropping toward freezing and water condensing on the walls, and the men were allowed only a few ounces of water each day to protect the cooling systems, which left Haise with a fever and a painful infection and left all three exhausted, dehydrated and sleeping little. Lovell lost around fourteen pounds over the course of the flight.

On the ground, Mattingly and teams of engineers worked in simulators through the night to write a procedure for turning Odyssey back on, a job that had never been planned for, in a sequence that had to bring up the systems one by one without drawing more power than the remaining batteries could supply. The crew also had to correct their course with small burns made by hand, using the Sun and then the terminator of the Earth to align the spacecraft, because the guidance platform had been shut down to save power, and the whole path of the ship came down to whether they could hold it steady through a narrow re-entry corridor that was only a few degrees wide. A few hours before the end the service module was jettisoned, and as it drifted away the astronauts saw for the first time how much of its side was missing, which explained why the spacecraft had lost so much so quickly. Aquarius was kept until the last possible moment, to be released shortly before entry, having done a job it was never built to do.

Re-entry began on April 17, and the blackout of radio contact caused by the plasma around the capsule stretched a little beyond the expected length, so that for a few extra moments in Houston and aboard the recovery ship nobody could say whether the heat shield had held, until Swigert's voice came through, and soon afterward Odyssey was swaying beneath three orange-and-white parachutes toward the South Pacific. It touched down near Samoa at about one in the afternoon Houston time after almost six days in space, and the three men were lifted aboard the helicopter and delivered to the deck of the carrier Iwo Jima, tired and unshaven but unharmed. An investigation led by Edgar Cortright found the cause in the tank and its heater system, NASA redesigned the tanks, removed the offending wiring and added a third oxygen tank placed apart from the others, and the flights resumed the following year. The mission has been remembered since as a success of improvisation, the Moon landing that never happened and a rescue that did.
